content:
Hold On Until the Last Moment

"To be honest, I held on until the very last moment." Ms. Yuen and her elder sister grew up with their parents at Wang Fuk Court. After her father passed away and her sister got married, Ms. Yuen lived with her mother until the devastating fire. Her mother lost her life in the blaze. In the period following the tragedy, she once wore a sweater with the handwritten words "rebuild on the original site" to voice her demands. Yet officials rejected the proposal, the owners' corporation refused to discuss it, and just one week before the 31 August acquisition deadline, she submitted a letter accepting the buyout offer.

Ms. Yuen believes residents of Wang Fuk Court have been forced into an impossible position. She said the two briefing officers she dealt with were unable to answer her questions and had only one clear objective — pressing neighbours on whether they had sold their flats.

Post-Disaster Life Feels Like "Being a Guest in Someone Else's Home"

Since the fire, Ms. Yuen has moved from Shin Lau in Tai Po to Yu Ying Lau in Aberdeen, paying a monthly "temporary residence fee" each month. The bed, dining table and TV cabinet that once belonged in the flat, along with the neighbours and security guards, constantly remind her of her status. She describes her life after the incident as "being a guest in someone else's home."

Rethinking What "Home" Really Means

She returns to the empty flat at eight or nine o'clock every evening after work, and on days off chooses to leave and stay at her sister's place. "Since it happened, I've been thinking — what do we mean by 'home'? A home is supposed to be a safe place, but when the home that was Wang Fuk Court could be burned down like that..."

"'Home' Is a Heavy Word for Me Now"

When the reporter asked Ms. Yuen about her vision of home, she said the old phone containing her photos of Wang Fuk Court was also lost in the fire, and all the memories now exist only in her mind. She sighed deeply and said: "It's not just about having a bed, a wardrobe, a bedroom, all the appliances perfectly in place — that alone doesn't make a proper home. It's made me rethink what elements truly make up a proper home, so I can't answer this question yet. Because right now, the word 'home' is quite heavy for me."

Resentful of Officials' "Letting Go" Remarks

The response of senior officials to the Wang Fuk Court fire — such as Chief Secretary for Administration Deputy Cheuk Wing-hing's remarks about "letting go" and Financial Secretary Deputy Wong Wai-lun's comments about market value — has fuelled her sense of helplessness and anger. "The more silent they are, the less I understand," she said. "When they can say something so cold and unfeeling, what does 'home' actually mean to them?"

A Sense of Being "Sold Off Cheaply"

Ms. Yuen recalled that the strongest emotions at the moment she signed the acceptance letter were unwillingness and a sense of injustice — a feeling of being "sold off cheaply" — because a home is not just about monetary value, but also about emotional and memory connections. "The flat was something my father and mother worked so hard for. If it really has to be taken from us for nothing, I'd rather not than feel it's being 'sold off cheaply' — I feel even more unwilling."

After signing the letter, Ms. Yuen will lose her status as an owner. The independent committee has postponed submitting its report until October. Ms. Yuen said holding people accountable is part of it, "but as for how I personally move on, I can't answer. Because from the incident until now, life feels like a total loss — first, the home was burned down, and what that burning meant was that the history of my growing up has been erased. A family member also died in the fire, and so suddenly... There's a huge hole in my heart. Can that hole truly be filled? Or will it one day heal? I don't know how to answer."
